summary: Defines a standard framework for extensible SNMP agents, where subagents handle parts of the management data and a master agent combines them. It is a standards-track document at the draft standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: SNMP agents are usually one program that answers every management question about a device. This RFC defines a way to split that job: one program, the master agent, answers the manager, and other programs, called subagents, hold the actual data. A protocol called AgentX connects them.

subtitle: How one SNMP agent can be built from many independent subagents behind a single master agent.

tldr.problem: Managed devices are often a collection of separately installed components, each with its own instrumentation. The SNMP framework does not describe how an agent's set of managed objects can be changed dynamically, so vendors invented incompatible ways of extending agents.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines master agents and subagents, the AgentX protocol they use to talk to each other, the PDU formats and encodings, and the elements of procedure for handling SNMP messages. A subagent registers the part of the MIB tree it holds, and the master agent dispatches requests to it.
tldr.outcome: Independently developed master agents and subagents can interoperate at the protocol level, and a manager cannot tell the difference between an extensible agent and a monolithic one. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2257.

today: RFC 2741 is a Draft Standard published in January 2000. It obsoletes RFC 2257, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the RFC Defines
sections.content:
RFC 2741 defines a standardized framework for extensible SNMP agents. It defines processing entities called master agents and subagents, a protocol, AgentX, used to communicate between them, and the elements of procedure by which the extensible agent processes SNMP protocol messages. The memo obsoletes RFC 2257.

The RFC notes that most of the changes from RFC 2257 are for the purpose of clarification, and that only two kinds of change affect the AgentX protocol messages on the wire. The agentx-Notify-PDU and agentx-Close-PDU now generate an agentx-Response-PDU, and three new error codes are available: parseFailed(266), requestDenied(267) and processingError(268).

The SNMP Management Framework that AgentX sits inside has five major components, as listed in Section 2: an overall architecture (RFC 2571); mechanisms for describing and naming objects, in SMIv1 (STD 16, RFC 1155, RFC 1212 and RFC 1215) and SMIv2 (STD 58, RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580); message protocols, in SNMPv1 (STD 15, RFC 1157), SNMPv2c (RFC 1901 and RFC 1906) and SNMPv3 (RFC 1906, RFC 2572 and RFC 2574); protocol operations for accessing management information, first in STD 15 and RFC 1157 and then in RFC 1905; and a set of fundamental applications (RFC 2573) with the view-based access control mechanism (RFC 2575).
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP agents are usually one program that answers every management question about a device. This RFC defines a way to split that job: one program, the master agent, answers the manager, and other programs, called subagents, hold the actual data. A protocol called AgentX connects them.

sections.title: Why AgentX Was Needed
sections.content:
New MIB modules that extend the Internet-standard MIB are continuously being defined by IETF working groups, and it is common for enterprises or individuals to create or extend enterprise-specific or experimental MIBs. As a result, managed devices are frequently complex collections of manageable components that have been independently installed on a managed node, each providing instrumentation for the managed objects defined in the MIB modules it implements. The SNMP framework does not describe how the set of managed objects supported by a particular agent may be changed dynamically.

This need has given rise to a variety of extensible agents, which typically comprise a master agent that is available on the standard transport address and accepts SNMP protocol messages; a set of subagents that each contain management instrumentation; a protocol that operates between the master agent and the subagents, permitting subagents to connect to the master agent and the master agent to multiplex received SNMP protocol messages amongst the subagents; and a set of tools to aid subagent development, together with a runtime environment that hides much of the protocol operation between a subagent and the master agent.

The RFC's argument is economic as much as technical. The wide deployment of extensible SNMP agents, coupled with the lack of Internet standards in this area, makes it difficult to field SNMP-manageable applications: a vendor may have to support several different subagent environments in order to support different target platforms, and it can become cumbersome to configure subagents and possibly multiple master agents on a particular managed node. Specifying a standard protocol for agent extensibility provides the technical foundation to solve both problems, so that independently developed AgentX-capable master agents and subagents can interoperate at the protocol level, while vendors continue to differentiate their products in all other respects.
sections.plainLanguage: Devices often carry software that was installed separately, each with its own monitoring data. The SNMP framework has no rule for adding management objects to a running agent, so vendors built their own ways to do it, and those ways did not work together. The RFC's argument is that a standard protocol lets independently written master agents and subagents work together.

sections.title: Master Agent and Subagent
sections.content:
Within the SNMP framework a managed node contains a processing entity, called an agent, which has access to management information. Within the AgentX framework an agent is further defined to consist of a single processing entity called the master agent, which sends and receives SNMP protocol messages in an agent role but typically has little or no direct access to management information, and zero or more processing entities called subagents, which are shielded from the SNMP protocol messages processed by the master agent but which have access to management information. The two communicate via AgentX protocol messages.

The RFC warns that although some AgentX protocol messages appear similar in syntax and semantics to SNMP, AgentX is not SNMP. The internal operations of AgentX are invisible to an SNMP entity operating in a manager role: from a manager's point of view, an extensible agent behaves exactly as a non-extensible, monolithic agent with access to the same management instrumentation. This transparency to managers is a fundamental requirement of AgentX, and it is what differentiates AgentX subagents from SNMP proxy agents.

Section 4.1 lists the functions of each role. The master agent accepts AgentX session establishment requests from subagents, accepts registration of MIB regions, sends and accepts SNMP protocol messages on the agent's transport addresses, implements the agent role elements of procedure except where they specify performing management operations, provides instrumentation for the MIB objects defined in RFC 1907, sends and receives AgentX protocol messages based on the current registry of MIB regions, and forwards notifications on behalf of subagents. The subagent initiates AgentX sessions, registers MIB regions, instantiates managed objects, binds OIDs within its registered regions to actual variables, performs management operations on variables, and initiates notifications.

Section 4.3 gives the design features. The primary one is a general division of labour: the master agent is MIB ignorant and SNMP omniscient, while the subagent is SNMP ignorant and MIB omniscient for the variables it instantiates. The others are a standard protocol and rules of engagement, mechanisms for independently developed subagents to integrate without awareness of any other subagent, a simple and deterministic registry and dispatching algorithm in which a single subagent is authoritative for any particular region of the MIB, and performance considerations, since the master agent and subagents are likely to reside on the same host. The design decisions that follow from that include 32-bit alignment of data within PDUs, native byte-order encoding by subagents, and large AgentX PDU payload sizes.

Section 4.4 records the non-goals. Subagent-to-subagent communication is out of scope, because of the security ramifications and complexity involved. Subagent access through the master agent to MIB variables is not addressed, since other mechanisms are available. And AgentX does not accommodate every conceivable extensible agent configuration option: the RFC states that some features in commercial extensible agent products are not included, because the consensus was that they were not appropriate for an Internet Standard, or not typically required for independently developed subagents to coexist. The set of supported configurations is the one described in Section 4.2, and some possible future version of the protocol may cover one or more of these non-goals.
sections.plainLanguage: The master agent handles SNMP itself and knows nothing about the MIB. Each subagent knows its part of the MIB and knows nothing about SNMP. The master agent sends the subagent a request naming the object, and the subagent answers. A manager cannot tell the difference between an extensible agent and a single-program agent with the same data.

sections.title: The AgentX PDU Header and Encodings
sections.content:
AgentX PDUs consist of a common header followed by PDU-specific data of variable length. Unlike SNMP PDUs, AgentX PDUs are not encoded using BER, but are transmitted as a contiguous byte stream. The data within the stream is organized to provide natural alignment with respect to the start of the PDU, permitting direct integer access by the processing entities. The first four fields in the header are single-byte values, and a bit in the third field, h.flags, indicates the byte ordering of all multi-byte integer values in the PDU, including those in the header itself.

The header is a fixed-format, 20-octet structure with these fields.

  • h.version: the version of the AgentX protocol, 1 for this memo.
  • h.type: the PDU type, one of eighteen values from agentx-Open-PDU (1) to agentx-Response-PDU (18). The types for administrative processing are 1 to 4 and 12 to 17; the types for SNMP request processing are 5 to 11.
  • h.flags: a bitmask with bit 0 the least significant bit. Bit 0 is INSTANCE_REGISTRATION, bit 1 is NEW_INDEX, bit 2 is ANY_INDEX, bit 3 is NON_DEFAULT_CONTEXT and bit 4 is NETWORK_BYTE_ORDER, with bits 5 to 7 reserved. If NETWORK_BYTE_ORDER is set, network byte order, most significant byte first, is used for every multi-byte integer in the whole packet; if it is not set, least significant byte first is used.
  • h.sessionID: uniquely identifies a session over which AgentX PDUs are exchanged between a subagent and the master agent. It has no significance in the agentx-Open-PDU; the master agent assigns one and passes it back in the corresponding response, and from then on the same value appears in every PDU of that session. A subagent may open several sessions.
  • h.transactionID: uniquely identifies, for a given session, the single SNMP management request with which an AgentX PDU is associated. It is not the same as the SNMP PDU request-id or the SNMP message msgID, since a master agent might receive SNMP requests with the same request-ids from different managers. It has no significance in administrative PDUs.
  • h.packetID: generated by the sender for all AgentX PDUs except the agentx-Response-PDU, whose packet ID must equal that of the PDU it responds to.
  • h.payload_length: the size in octets of the PDU contents, excluding the 20-byte header. Because of the encoding schemes and PDU layouts, this value is always either 0 or a multiple of 4.

Section 5 defines the encodings. An object identifier is a 4-byte header followed by a variable number of contiguous 4-byte sub-identifier fields; a null object identifier consists of the 4-byte header with all bytes set to 0. A SearchRange consists of two object identifiers: the starting OID, whose include field says whether the starting OID is in the range, and the ending OID, whose include field is always 0 and whose null value indicates an unbounded range. An octet string is a contiguous series of bytes beginning with a 4-byte length, with padding bytes appended so that following data stays on a 4-byte boundary; the padding must be added even if the octet string is the last item in the PDU, and padding bytes must be zero filled.
sections.plainLanguage: Every AgentX message starts with a fixed 20-byte header. It names the protocol version, the kind of message, which session it belongs to, which request it answers, and how long the rest of the message is. A flag in the header says whether the numbers that follow are written with the most significant byte first or the least significant byte first.

sections.title: The Eighteen AgentX PDUs
sections.content:
Section 6.2 defines the eighteen PDUs. The administrative ones cover session and registration management. The agentx-Open-PDU is generated by a subagent to request establishment of a session, and carries a timeout, an object identifier identifying the subagent and a description. The agentx-Close-PDU is sent by a subagent to terminate a session. The agentx-Register-PDU is generated by a subagent for each region of the MIB variable naming tree, within one or more contexts, that it wishes to support; it carries an optional context, a timeout that applies only to messages concerning objects in that subtree, a priority between 1 and 255, and the subtree itself. The agentx-Unregister-PDU withdraws such a registration.

The SNMP request processing PDUs mirror the SNMP operations. There are agentx-Get-PDU, agentx-GetNext-PDU, agentx-GetBulk-PDU and agentx-TestSet-PDU, plus the agentx-CommitSet-PDU, agentx-UndoSet-PDU and agentx-CleanupSet-PDU, which together form the two-phase set sequence. The agentx-Notify-PDU carries a notification, the agentx-Ping-PDU tests that a session is alive, the agentx-IndexAllocate-PDU and agentx-IndexDeallocate-PDU manage shared table indexes, and the agentx-AddAgentCaps-PDU and agentx-RemoveAgentCaps-PDU manage the capabilities of a session.

Every one of them is answered by an agentx-Response-PDU, whose res.error field carries the status. For responses to administrative PDUs the values are limited to a list of thirteen: noAgentXError (0), openFailed (256), notOpen (257), indexWrongType (258), indexAlreadyAllocated (259), indexNoneAvailable (260), indexNotAllocated (261), unsupportedContext (262), duplicateRegistration (263), unknownRegistration (264), unknownAgentCaps (265), parseError (266), requestDenied (267) and processingError (268). For responses to SNMP request processing PDUs the values may also include those defined for errors in the SNMPv2 PDU of RFC 1905. The res.index field gives, in error cases, the index of the failed variable binding within the received request PDU.
sections.plainLanguage: There are 18 kinds of message. Some open and close sessions, and some register a part of the MIB tree with the master agent. Others carry the SNMP operations themselves, such as Get, GetNext, GetBulk and TestSet. Each kind has a matching response message, and the responses carry an error code when something goes wrong.

sections.title: Elements of Procedure
sections.content:
Section 7 describes the actions of master agents and subagents implementing the protocol. The administrative messages are processed first. A subagent opens a session with an agentx-Open-PDU, and the master agent assigns a session ID and replies. The subagent then registers the regions it supports. The master agent keeps a registry of MIB regions, and for a given configuration there is a single subagent that is authoritative for any particular region, which may extend from an entire MIB down to a single object instance.

Because registrations overlap, the master agent's dispatching algorithm selects an authoritative region in a fixed order. It chooses the registration whose original agentx-Register-PDU carried the most sub-identifiers, that is, the most specific subtree; the presence or absence of a range sub-identifier has no bearing on that comparison. If that is still ambiguous, because there were duplicate subtrees, it chooses the one whose original agentx-Register-PDU specified the smaller value of r.priority. A priority is a value between 1 and 255, and subagents with no particular knowledge of priority should register with the default value of 127.

The master agent also provides index allocation as a service. It maintains a database of index objects, and for each index the values allocated for it, and it is unaware of what MIB variables the index objects represent. By convention subagents use the MIB variable listed in the INDEX clause as the index object for which values must be allocated, which gives generic support for sharing MIB conceptual tables among subagents who have no knowledge of each other.

For SNMP requests, the master agent dispatches the AgentX PDU to the subagent that owns the object, and processes the responses that come back. Subagents process agentx-Get, GetNext and GetBulk PDUs, and the TestSet, CommitSet, UndoSet and CleanupSet PDUs, and the master agent applies MIB views and access control, which the subagents are not aware of because view information is not contained in AgentX PDUs.

Section 7.3 gives the state transitions. The Set transaction states are shown from the subagent's perspective, with five states: an initial state, TestOK, CommitOK, TestFail and CommitFail. On receiving a TestSet PDU the subagent moves to TestOK if all variable bindings pass and to TestFail if not. On receiving a CommitSet PDU it moves to CommitOK or CommitFail. An UndoSet PDU ends a CommitOK or CommitFail transaction, and a CleanupSet PDU ends a TestOK, CommitOK or TestFail one. Session loss ends any of them. The RFC notes the three possible sequences a subagent may follow for a particular set transaction: TestSet CommitSet CleanupSet, TestSet CommitSet UndoSet, and TestSet CleanupSet. The transport connection and session establishment states are shown from the master agent's perspective.
sections.plainLanguage: A subagent opens a session, then registers the part of the MIB tree it holds, giving a priority number and optionally a time limit. The master agent keeps a registry of these registrations. When a manager asks for an object, the master agent finds the registration that covers it and sends the request to that subagent. For a write, the subagent first tests the new values, then commits them, and can undo or clean up if the test fails.

sections.title: Transport Mappings
sections.content:
The same AgentX PDU formats, encodings and elements of procedure are used regardless of the underlying transport. The RFC defines two mappings.

Over TCP, the master agent accepts connection requests for the well-known port 705, and subagents connect to it using that port number. Once a TCP connection has been established, the AgentX peers use it to carry all AgentX PDUs. Multiple AgentX sessions may be established over the same TCP connection, and the peers are responsible for mapping the session ID to a particular connection. The AgentX entity must not interleave PDUs within the byte stream: all the bytes of one PDU must be sent before any bytes of a different PDU, and the receiving entity must be prepared for TCP to deliver byte sequences that do not coincide with PDU boundaries.

Over UNIX-domain sockets, the master agent creates a well-known endpoint called /var/agentx/master, and may create other, implementation-specific endpoints. The endpoint name uses the character set encoding native to the managed node and represents a UNIX-domain stream socket. The RFC says the mapping is useful for environments that wish to guarantee that subagents run on the same managed node as the master agent, and where sockets provide better performance than TCP or UDP, especially in the presence of heavy network I/O. The rules about not interleaving PDUs and about being prepared for arbitrary byte sequences apply here too.
sections.plainLanguage: The same messages work over any transport. The RFC defines two mappings: TCP, where the master agent listens on port 705, and UNIX-domain sockets, where the master agent creates an endpoint at /var/agentx/master. A master agent can carry several sessions over one connection.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo defines a protocol between two processing entities, one of which, the master agent, is assumed to perform authentication of received SNMP requests and to control access to management information. The master agent performs those security operations independently of the other entity, the subagent.

The RFC frames the security questions as three. First, is a particular subagent allowed to initiate a session with a particular master agent? Second, during a session, is any SNMP security-related information, for example community names, passed from the master agent to the subagent? Third, during a session, what part of the MIB tree is this subagent allowed to register?

The answer to the third is that a subagent can register any subtree, subject to the elements of procedure, and that there is currently no access control mechanism defined in AgentX. The RFC states the concern: a malicious subagent that registers an unauthorized sensitive subtree could see modification requests to those objects, or, by giving clever answers to queries, could cause a network management system to do something that leads to information disclosure or other damage. The answer to the second question is no.

For the first question, AgentX contains no mechanism for authorizing or refusing session initiations, so controlling subagent access to the master agent may only be done at a lower layer, such as the transport. Where a local transport mechanism is used and both subagent and master agent run on the same host, connection authorization can be delegated to the operating system, and the answer becomes that the operating system will allow the connection if and only if the subagent has sufficient privileges. If a network transport is used, the RFC states that there is currently no inherent security, and that Transport Layer Security, SSL or IPsec SHOULD be used to control and protect subagent connections in that mode. It also RECOMMENDS that subagents always run on the same host as the master agent, and that operating system features be used to ensure that only properly authorized subagents can establish connections.
sections.plainLanguage: AgentX has no mechanism of its own for deciding which subagents may connect, so that has to be enforced by the transport or the operating system. The RFC recommends that subagents run on the same host as the master agent so the operating system can control access, and that TLS or IPsec be used if a network transport is used. It also notes there is no access control on which parts of the MIB a subagent may register.
